This study introduces a novel category of high-order time integration schemes designed specifically for structural dynamics within the context of isogeometric analysis. These methods are founded on the generalized-$\alpha$ approach, which is renowned for its capability to dampen high-frequency numerical artifacts while preserving physical low-frequency behavior. The proposed techniques are derived through the application of a modified $\beta$-method to the governing equations of motion. The integration process employs a unique strategy for determining the coefficients, which relies on the relationship between the polynomial order of the finite element shape functions and the integration parameters. This approach ensures that the resulting methods maintain the accuracy inherent in the underlying isogeometric formulation. The developed algorithms are validated through numerical experiments that assess their performance in structural dynamics problems.

The Bose polaron, representing a fermionic impurity coupled to a bath of bosons, serves as a crucial system for investigating many-body interactions in ultracold atomic gases. While prior research has largely focused on its properties within a single quantum well, this study examines the dynamics of the residual polaron population as the fermionic bath is cooled by transitioning from one to two quantum wells. We demonstrate that the time-dependent polaron decay is driven by two distinct mechanisms: the breaking of intra- and inter-band excitations. Furthermore, we analyze how the ratio of intra-to-interband excitations depends on the coupling strength, revealing that intra-band decay dominates the short-time regime, whereas inter-band decay governs the long-time behavior. These findings are validated through exact diagonalization calculations.

Disaster relief logistics planning is a pivotal challenge for emergency response, characterized by significant uncertainty regarding the timing, location, and scale of events. Consequently, this paper introduces a multi-stage stochastic programming framework designed to determine optimal pre- and post-disaster strategies for dispatching relief supplies. The model explicitly accounts for dynamic, time-dependent factors such as fluctuating demand, evolving road accessibility, and shifting transportation costs. To address the computational complexity of this approach, we develop a novel multi-stage decomposition algorithm that integrates the L-shaped method with forward simulation. This hybrid approach iteratively evaluates post-disaster scenarios to identify critical gaps between current and target objective values, subsequently refining the pre-disaster planning stage by adding constraints to address these deficiencies. The efficacy of this proposed method is validated through computational experiments using a real-world case study of the 2013 Typhoon Haiyan.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are expected to detect gravitational waves (GWs) generated by supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) residing in galactic centers. While the detection of GWs from eccentric binaries is anticipated to be more feasible than from circular ones, the resulting signals are intricate, necessitating high-precision waveform models. This study introduces a new PTAs-based signal model for inspiralling eccentric SMBHBs, achieving accuracy up to the 2.5 post-Newtonian (2.5PN) order. This model is validated against numerical relativity simulations and compared with existing approaches, revealing that it is more precise than prior models but slightly less computationally efficient. Furthermore, the impact of neglecting higher PN orders on the timing residuals is examined. The findings indicate that omitting these higher PN orders results in timing residual errors reaching approximately 100 nanoseconds for binaries with orbital periods of 100 days and eccentricities of 0.1 or greater. This error magnitude is substantial enough to potentially hinder the detection of eccentric binaries via PTAs.

This study examines a global game featuring risk-averse agents who observe a noisy signal regarding an uncertain global action. Agents face a choice between a risky payoff tied to whether a specific aggregate threshold is met and a fixed alternative. We analyze how the distribution of the signals' precision affects the probability that the critical threshold is exceeded. We find that while lower levels of signal noise generally increase the likelihood of success, this relationship is not linear; instead, it follows a non-monotonic pattern. This non-monotonicity arises because the threshold can fall within a range where the payoff function exhibits risk-loving characteristics, a scenario that is not uniform across all distributions of signal noise.

This study introduces a technique for measuring the dielectric properties of high-loss liquids within the 750 GHz to 1100 GHz range. The method utilizes a coplanar waveguide (CPW) with a suspended substrate, enabling direct on-chip measurement of the liquid. By analyzing the resulting transmission spectrum, the technique successfully determines the material's dielectric permittivity and loss tangent. The method's accuracy was validated against an independent reference approach, which involves suspending the liquid in air and measuring its response using a vector network analyzer. The results demonstrate that this approach can achieve measurement precision of approximately 1% for the real part and 5% for the imaginary part of the dielectric function.

The AIRSENSE-TO-ACT initiative, led by the University of Bologna, aims to develop a comprehensive framework for monitoring and analyzing the COVID-19 pandemic. This project integrates diverse data streams—including air quality metrics, meteorological conditions, and mobility patterns—to create a robust, multi-source data platform. Leveraging this platform, the system will employ machine learning algorithms to generate a predictive model for the disease's spread, thereby offering actionable insights for public health officials and policymakers. Ultimately, the initiative seeks to enhance the quality of decision-making regarding countermeasures and support the formulation of effective public health strategies.

This paper introduces a multi-resolution SPH formulation designed to address fluid-structure interactions. The method employs a continuous approximation of the kernel function, ensuring smoothness in the pressure gradient and reducing numerical artifacts. Additionally, the study implements a multi-phase approach utilizing a density-based interface capturing technique. The proposed model is validated through simulations involving a pendulum and a falling plate interacting with a two-phase flow. The results demonstrate that the method effectively resolves the complex dynamics of multi-phase fluid-structure interactions.

Nodal lines within momentum space represent one-dimensional, line-like degeneracies occurring between energy bands. These structures are topologically protected, characterized by non-trivial topological invariants that prevent their removal under continuous deformations. This review examines the topological attributes of these nodal lines, highlighting their physical manifestations in recent studies across various platforms. Particular focus is placed on how advanced topological invariants dictate the specific interactions between these nodal lines and external perturbations. Furthermore, the article explores the implementation of nodal lines in photonic systems, demonstrating their utility for light manipulation and optical device engineering.

This document outlines the anticipated demands for event generation software within the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) environment. It examines the specific computing and system-architecture requirements necessary to facilitate this software in the upcoming stage-3 of the LHC program. The text also explores the integration of these tools into the broader analysis framework, covering associated computing needs and the potential impact on workflow efficiency.

We present a new study of the outer Galaxy's dark molecular gas, utilizing the 12CO J=1-0 line data from the Galactic Legacy All-Sky Survey (GLASS). Our analysis reveals a substantial, previously unrecognized reservoir of molecular material, characterized by a scale height of approximately 1.5 kpc and a total mass of roughly 1.5 x 10^7 solar masses. This "dark disk" is distinguished from the standard molecular disk by its greater thickness, lower surface density, and a velocity dispersion that is nearly twice as high. The mass of this dark disk accounts for about 20% of the total molecular gas mass in the Galaxy. Our findings suggest that this dark disk is a product of the merger of the Milky Way with a satellite galaxy possessing a comparable mass.

This study examines the strategic interactions between wage-setters and firms within a closed economy, where firms operate under a constraint to maximize profits. The analysis demonstrates that the resulting Nash equilibrium yields wage-optimal levels, and these findings are supported by numerical simulations.

This study investigates the collective behavior of dense polar active matter composed of self-propelled particles with fixed orientations in a two-dimensional plane. We examine the active Brownian swimmer model, which accounts for both rotational diffusion and a finite persistence length. By applying a hydrodynamic framework, we derive a dynamical equation for the active density $\rho(\mathbf{r},t)$, which incorporates a velocity-dependent advective term, a diffusion term, and a source term representing self-propulsion. This hydrodynamic equation is solved using a perturbative approach, yielding a closed-form expression for the dynamic structure factor $S(k,z)$. This result is validated against numerical simulations, revealing that the active diffusion coefficient $D_a$ decreases as the active Péclet number ($Pe_{act}$) increases. Furthermore, we observe that the active source term scales with density as $\rho^2$ and depends on $Pe_{act}$, exhibiting a non-monotonic trend with respect to $k$. These findings underscore the critical role of $Pe_{act}$ in shaping the collective dynamics of active systems.

This study introduces a novel approach to localization that leverages dialogue with a human agent. Our method utilizes a natural language interface to gather responses from the agent, which describe objects within an agent-centered spatial context. These descriptions are then parsed to extract object locations relative to the initiator and a surrounding scene graph. By integrating these individual object locations, we construct a comprehensive scene graph for localization. We evaluate this methodology across two datasets: a synthetic one and an indoor localization dataset featuring a real-world human-agent interaction. Our results demonstrate that our approach achieves performance on par with current state-of-the-art localization techniques.

This paper introduces a new methodology for automatically selecting frequency bands in vibration analysis, designed to enhance the effectiveness of machine learning techniques in fault diagnosis. The proposed approach, termed Band Relevance Factor (BRF), is intended to improve the discriminative power of features extracted from vibration data. By applying the BRf to a dataset of rotating machinery vibration signals, the study demonstrates that this method yields feature sets that are more distinct and informative than those derived from standard frequency domain analysis.

We report muon-spin relaxation and rotation (μSR) findings for the noncentrosymmetric superconductors CaIrSi₃ and CaPtSi₃, both exhibiting Tc values of 4.5 K and 4.1 K, respectively. Our zero-field μSR data reveal a two-component order parameter with a gap structure resembling that of a triplet superconductor. Furthermore, the zero-temperature internal field distribution derived from the internal field width is broad, indicating a finite distribution of muon sites. This broadness is attributed to the lack of inversion symmetry in these materials, which generates local electric fields that mix electronic states of opposite parity. Consequently, the observed superconducting state is interpreted as a superposition of singlet and triplet components.

This study introduces a novel approach to solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for stochastic optimal control problems, leveraging a sparse grid characteristic technique. By combining the PDE representation of the value function with a nonlinear control transformation, we convert the original HJB equation into a system of algebraic equations. This transformation relies on a specific structure within the control space, enabling the application of a sparse grid method to effectively circumvent the curse of dimensionality. The paper demonstrates the efficacy of this sparse grid method through two benchmark problems: the linear quadratic regulator and a nonlinear system featuring both linear and quadratic terms.

We propose a classification framework for characterizing general quantum measurements applied to single-qubit and single-qudit systems. This method utilizes the convex hull of an asymmetric, real-valued function derived from an arbitrary measurement operator set, defined as the "measuring polytope." The geometric attributes of this polytope determine the classification of a measurement, with specific facets of the polytope corresponding to extreme binary measurements. We demonstrate that the vertices of the polytope correspond precisely to extreme binary measurements, thereby establishing a link between the geometric structure of the measuring polytope and the measurement classification problem. Furthermore, we present a method for reconstructing the measuring polytope from experimental data, enabling the classification of a measurement based solely on its observed vertices. Finally, we apply the measuring polytope to the task of optimal cloning of single-qudit pure states, revealing that the maximal cloning fidelity for a symmetric universal cloning machine is achieved when the cloner is symmetric.

This study introduces a novel framework for managing multi-energy dynamical systems, defined by the interconnection of multiple energy domains—such as electricity, heat, and gas—through shared physical components like transformers, heat pumps, and electric vehicles. We present a new modeling approach that represents these interconnected systems as a single, unified domain, utilizing a specialized energy storage concept termed "energy batteries." These batteries encapsulate energy stored in thermal mass, pressurized fluids, or chemical bonds, enabling the application of established electrical control techniques to this unified system. We demonstrate the practical value of this approach by applying a classical electrical controller to a complex network involving electricity, gas, and heating. Furthermore, we analyze the system's stability under various operating conditions and validate our findings through simulations.

We investigate the two-dimensional percolation model, which serves as a fundamental paradigm for phase transitions in statistical physics. By employing machine learning techniques, we construct a neural network capable of predicting the percolation probability based on the density of occupied sites. This approach successfully recovers the critical density $\rho_c$ with remarkable precision, yielding a percolation probability estimate of $0.5927 \pm 0.0030$ for an infinite lattice size. Additionally, the finite-size scaling behavior of the percolation threshold is derived from the model's output.

The method utilizes a $T_1$-weighted MRI sequence, where the relaxation time $T_1$ serves as a direct indicator of temperature. By applying a sequence of low-power radiofrequency pulses, we achieve high temporal resolution without compromising signal quality. The system's precision was validated using a calibration experiment with water, which yielded a temperature accuracy of $\pm 0.1$ K. We introduce a phenomenological framework for superconductivity featuring quenched disorder and thermal fluctuations, applicable to systems like UTe$_2$. This model examines how such quenched disorder influences the superconducting phase diagram, specifically analyzing the effects of disorder on the critical temperature ($T_c$) and superconducting fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that disorder can induce a reentrant superconducting state within the normal phase, a phenomenon we attribute to the suppression of fluctuations in specific regions of the phase diagram. This reentrant behavior is observed across a range of disorder strengths and is accompanied by a distinct peak in the superconducting transition width. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the specific heat jump at $T_c$ diminishes with increasing disorder. Finally, we propose that the disorder-induced reentrant superconductivity may also manifest in superconducting fullerenes.

Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is an emerging wireless standard designed for short-range, low-power data transmission. It is widely adopted in various sectors, including industrial automation, healthcare, and consumer electronics, where it serves as a reliable communication solution. However, UWB's performance is heavily dependent on the specific physical environment, which can be unpredictable and change over time. To address this, UWB systems must adapt to fluctuating channel conditions to maintain optimal performance. This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to automate real-time adjustments of UWB physical layer (PHY) parameters. The study details the design of the DRL agent and evaluates its effectiveness in optimizing key PHY settings, specifically transmit power and bandwidth. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed DRL approach outperforms traditional heuristic methods, achieving superior efficiency and adaptability in dynamic environments.

This paper investigates the k-median clustering problem within the context of geometric string and curve distances, specifically focusing on the Discrete Fr\'e\'e chet (DF) and Hausdorff (H) metrics. We introduce and analyze a novel algorithm that merges the core principles of the k-median clustering framework with the structural characteristics of DF and H distances. Theoretically, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(k + \min\{\sigma_1, \sigma_2\})$ for the approximation ratio of our approach, where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ represent the maximum distances between any pair of the $k$ medians and between any pair of the input strings or curves, respectively. Furthermore, we prove that this bound is tight for DF clustering by demonstrating an upper bound of $O(k + \sigma_1 + \sigma_2)$. The proposed method is also proven to be optimal, as its approximation ratio converges to $O(k)$ when $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are constant.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has become a prominent approach for addressing complex, large-scale optimization problems. However, the inherent non-stationarity of the learning environment, driven by the evolving strategies of other agents, significantly hinders the convergence of MARL algorithms. This study introduces a novel MARL framework that leverages the principles of convex optimization. By modeling the learning process as a convex-concave min-max problem, the method employs a double-averaging technique within a primal-dual optimization algorithm to determine the saddle point. This strategy effectively mitigates the non-stationarity issue, thereby enhancing the convergence rate of the proposed MARL algorithm. Theoretical analysis confirms that the method achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality bound, where $T$ represents the number of iterations. Additionally, the method is evaluated on two benchmark tasks: the classic matrix game and a variant of the game of chicken. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of convergence speed and solution quality.

We introduce a coalgebraic framework designed for the satisfiability verification of $\mu$-calculi that incorporate arithmetic. Our framework establishes a general method for constructing satisfiability trees, proving a general satisfiability result, and providing a unified approach to representing $\mu$-calculi with non-deterministic choice. This method is applied to three specific variants: the $\mu$-calculus with LTL, the $\mu$-calculus with LTL under fair semantics, and the $\mu$-calculus with LTL under justifications. Additionally, we outline a general strategy for implementing this framework within Coq, and we demonstrate a concrete implementation of the tree-based satisfiability test for the $\mu$-calculus with LTL.

This study introduces a technique for recovering the initial state of nonlinear wave equations, utilizing the specific characteristics of the solution. The proposed methodology comprises two distinct stages. Initially, we determine a low-rank approximation of the solution at the current time point by applying the method of characteristics to the governing PDE. Subsequently, we employ a nonlinear optimization approach to derive the initial condition, utilizing the low-rank approximation obtained in the first stage. This paper further establishes the convergence properties of the reconstruction algorithm and validates the method's effectiveness through various numerical experiments.

The proposed method integrates facility location theory to identify optimal sensor placement, thereby reducing the need for sensors in every vehicle. Instead, it utilizes the subset of vehicles that pass near facilities to estimate air quality for the remaining areas. The study evaluates the accuracy of this approach by comparing it against a baseline where sensors are installed in all vehicles. This paper establishes an Weil representation for the generalized linear group defined over a specific ring of truncated polynomials over a finite field, under the condition of possessing a second-class non-standard involutions.

Persuasive technologies are increasingly employed to influence human behavior, with persuasive video generation (PGV) emerging as a critical field within artificial intelligence. Although numerous AI-driven content creation methods have recently been introduced, there remains a lack of comprehensive surveys on the current status, challenges, and opportunities within PGV. This paper reviews existing persuasive video generation techniques, examines their underlying data sources, and identifies key hurdles and potential future directions. We also discuss the ethical implications of PGV and the associated risks. Ultimately, this survey aims to foster further research and development in PGV.

We examine the squeezed coherent states of motion for ions confined within quadrupole and octupole ion traps. Our findings reveal that the octupole trap exhibits a notable ability to significantly suppress ion heating.

Neuroscience models are increasingly intricate, making it essential to employ efficient hyper-parameter optimization methods. This study introduces a framework for such optimization that integrates the emerging "learning to learn" paradigm with established Bayesian optimization techniques. By utilizing historical data from prior models to initialize the predictive system, this approach accelerates the exploration of design spaces. We evaluated this framework against a suite of computational models from the neuroscience domain, including those simulating neural networks, synaptic plasticity, and neural mass dynamics. Results demonstrate that this method achieves a 100-fold reduction in the number of required simulations compared to standard Bayesian optimization and minimizes performance degradation to only 1.5% relative to the optimal solution. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the approach yields substantial benefits when applied to model spaces of moderate dimensions.

Camouflaged objects are defined by their blending into the background, a phenomenon that poses significant challenges for object segmentation. While numerous methods have been developed to address this, the scarcity of suitable datasets has hindered progress. In this work, we introduce the Camouflaged Instance Segmentation (CIS) dataset, which comprises 1,000 images featuring diverse camouflaged objects across various categories. We also present a benchmark suite consisting of four state-of-the-art segmentation methods to facilitate standardized performance evaluation. Furthermore, we propose a new approach that employs a dual-branch network to jointly detect object presence and delineate object boundaries. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing techniques on both the CIS dataset and the standard COCO dataset. We make the dataset and all benchmark resources publicly available to support future research.

As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in critical areas like healthcare and autonomous driving, ensuring their reliability and safety becomes paramount. This study introduces a new approach to systematically uncovering and validating errors in AI systems by leveraging crowdsourced failure reports. We developed a crowdsourcing platform designed to gather these reports, which were subsequently verified by annotators. Our analysis of the resulting dataset reveals that while the vast majority of submitted failures represent genuine issues, the current process generates a high volume of redundant submissions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these failure patterns are not random; they exhibit significant correlations with specific model and data characteristics. Ultimately, the dataset presented herein offers a valuable resource for advancing AI safety and robustness research.

We introduce a novel object detection framework that employs random decision routing to enhance performance. This approach utilizes a simple, novel, and computationally efficient method to assign proposals to multiple detectors, enabling them to specialize in different regions of the image. This strategy allows the network to learn more robust features, as it can focus on specific areas rather than attempting to generalize across the entire image. This specialization is particularly beneficial for small objects, which are often difficult to detect. This approach is compatible with any existing single-detection model, requiring no changes to the original architecture. We evaluated our method on the PASCAL VOC and MS Coco benchmarks, achieving a 1.2% increase in AP on MS Coco and a 0.6% increase on VOC compared to the original model. This approach is compatible with any existing single-detection model, requiring no changes to the original architecture. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, including those based on the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM). While adversarial training is a standard defense mechanism, it often results in catastrophic overfitting, where the model's accuracy on clean data drops significantly. This study introduces a novel approach, ZeroGrad, designed to mitigate such overfitting. The method employs a zero-gradient strategy to generate adversarial examples, thereby reducing catastrophic overfitting and enhancing overall model performance. ZeroGrad is evaluated against state-of-the-art adversarial training techniques on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. The results demonstrate that ZeroGrad achieves superior performance in resisting adversarial attacks while maintaining robust accuracy on clean data.

This study examines the Thakurta metric, a proposed solution to Einstein's equations for a cosmological black hole, and concludes that it fails to represent such objects. Consequently, limits on primordial black holes derived from gravitational wave signals produced by binary mergers are unaffected.

This study examines the convergence behavior of a specific class of optimization algorithms designed for hybrid systems, which are defined by their ability to switch between different smooth functions. These algorithms, which include the generalized method of multipliers and the generalized dual ascent method, are applied to a constrained optimization problem where the objective function is a sum of smooth non-convex terms and non-smooth convex regularizers, and feasible solutions must lie within a finite union of closed convex sets. The research demonstrates that the algorithm's iterates converge to a stationary point of the problem, which is characterized as the set of global minima for each individual smooth component. The analysis further reveals that the rate of convergence for the iterates approaching this stationary set is linear, provided specific conditions are met. These conditions involve assuming that the objective function exhibits the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz (KL) property and that the algorithms possess a "persistent switching" trait, meaning they are capable of toggling between the smooth functions. The latter requirement is shown to be naturally fulfilled by many practical applications, such as those in compressed sensing and phase retrieval.

Bootstrapping represents a critical challenge in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a field that enables computations on encrypted data. This paper introduces BTS, a novel bootstrapping framework designed for the BFV variant of FHE, leveraging the Kyber public-key system for its underlying structure. BTS employs a modular architecture that breaks down the bootstrapping process into three distinct stages: key switching, plaintext switching, and rekeying. By utilizing the inherent cryptographic primitives of Kyper, this approach offers significant flexibility and adaptability. Experimental results indicate that BTS achieves a 10-fold improvement in performance compared to the current state-of-the-art scheme, FHEW, while also demonstrating superior compatibility with the TFHE encryption scheme.

This work examines a random matrix ensemble featuring a logarithmic confining potential, $V(z) = \lambda \ln z^2$, where $\lambda$ is a parameter. We establish that the corresponding $R$-matrix kernel $G_N(z,w)$, which is determinantal, can be expressed using a Schur function multiplied by a Whittaker function. Furthermore, we derive a determinantal representation for the gap probability at specific points on the real axis. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of Whittaker functions, we determine the probability limits of gap events at infinity and on the real line. Additionally, we derive a differential equation governing the gap probability that is solvable via Whittaker functions, and we provide a derivation of a differential equation for the partition function. Finally, we investigate the large $\lambda$ limit of the gap probability, revealing that it converges to a solution of a Painlevé V equation.

This study experimentally investigates quantum correlations within a two-qutrit spin system using a pair of entangled calcium atoms. The researchers measured both quantum discord and entanglement witness (concurrence) in this multilevel setup. The results indicate that for this qutrit configuration, quantum discord remains significantly higher than concurrence across most configurations, with the exception of the maximally entangled state. The observed trends were validated by a quantitative model that incorporates the specific characteristics of the system, such as its excitation and measurement protocols, along with experimental imperfections like decoherence and detection inefficiency.

This study introduces a framework for modeling quantum correlations that remains consistent with both the relativity principle and causality while avoiding a fourth Bell's theorem. It posits that local quantum correlations arise from the entanglement of distant, non-commuting observables, which are linked to specific local variables. The framework's core innovation is the introduction of a "hidden" variable capable of representing the non-commutative nature of these observables. This hidden variable establishes a joint probability distribution for the non-commuting pair, which subsequently factorizes into measurable local probabilities conditioned on the hidden state. This mechanism allows the formalism to reproduce Bell's theorem while simultaneously deriving the Schrödinger equation for entangled pure states.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a video synthesis architecture that merges the high-quality image generation capabilities of StyleGAN2 with the continuous video generation features of StyleGAN-VAE. This model achieves state-of-the-art results on the YouTube-OSIS benchmark, surpassing previous records by 1.5 dB in FID score and 1.4 dB in LPIPS. Additionally, our method offers superior performance in video interpolation and domain adaptation compared to StyleGAN-VAE. The source code and pre-trained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/NVlabs/stylegan-v.

The text explores the relationship between the degree disparities of rational points on certain K3 surfaces and a specific subset of their étale cohomology. This research extends findings by Burns, Li, and Schreieder concerning the motivic weight conjectures, which apply to the full set of étale cohomology elements.

Accurate estimation of the exposure date is critical for radiation protection, particularly in emergency scenarios. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to determine these dates by analyzing the glow curves generated via thermolumuminescence (TL) measurements. The proposed method leverages the specific characteristics of TL curves, which vary based on the TL material's preheating duration. We evaluated the model's performance using a dataset of 1,000 glow curves captured by the TL-READ 2005A system. The results demonstrate that the deep learning approach significantly outperforms the traditional method of estimating exposure dates from preheating times.

This paper examines a category of double-phase problems characterized by a singular term, non-Lipschitz behavior, and a null set at infinity, defined over the product of an open subset within the non-compact unit sphere of the $n$-dimensional Euclidean manifold and the non-negative real line. By applying the Mountain Pass Theorem, we establish the existence of a weak solution to these problems.

The Fastcat simulator, developed by the University of Adelaide, models the CBCT system at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre (PMPMCP) in Melbourne, specifically for the kV OptiShape and MV iCBCT systems. This study validates the simulator's accuracy regarding the geometric and physical characteristics of the pMPMcb iCBR system. The research involved acquiring and processing real experimental datasets to create ground truth images, which were then compared against simulated outputs. Specifically, the validation focused on the geometric accuracy of the detector-to-isocenter distance, source-to-isocenter distance, and the X-ray focal spot's size and shape. Additionally, the spectral properties of the X-ray source were evaluated. The results confirmed that the simulator accurately represents the system's geometry and X-ray source properties, with a maximum deviation of 0.5 mm for the distances and 0.1 mm for the focal spot dimensions. The spectral validation showed a maximum deviation of 1.5% from the peak energy. These findings demonstrate the tool's high accuracy and its potential for clinical application.

Machine learning models are increasingly ubiquitous across diverse fields, yet their complex internal structures often render them opaque to human users. Consequently, numerous interpretability methods have emerged to address this issue, yet many existing solutions struggle with computational efficiency. This paper introduces a new approach that significantly enhances the speed of explanation generation. By leveraging the concept of "stability" to define the optimal region for local perturbations, our proposed method, S-LIME, substantially reduces the sample count required for LIME. This reduction leads to faster execution and improved interpretability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that S-LIME can be extended to create an even more efficient variant, OLS-LIME, which utilizes ordinary least squares to calculate feature attributions.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian framework designed to rectify misclassifications by leveraging expert feedback on explanations. The approach employs a generative model that integrates the classifier's internal parameters with its decision boundaries to simulate the classification process. By conditioning this model on erroneous predictions and corresponding expert-defined class characteristics, the framework derives a posterior distribution for the parameters, which serves as the basis for generating corrected predictions. The efficacy of this method is validated through extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, where it demonstrates superior performance compared to existing approaches.

We report on the discovery of crystal-field excitations in the spin-liquid candidate TbInO$_3$ using inelastic neutron scattering. These excitations are observed to be well-defined and exhibit a quasi-two-dimensional character, aligning with the material's structural symmetry. Furthermore, the neutron data reveal a broad, low-energy continuum that we attribute to vibronic modes arising from the excitation of oxygen atoms. This interpretation is supported by the continuum's strong temperature dependence and its sensitivity to magnetic field orientation. Additionally, the continuum's momentum distribution mirrors that of the crystal-field excitations, suggesting a strong vibronic coupling between the crystal-field states and the local oxygen vibrations.

We investigate the evolution of convex hypersurces under the flow governed by a power-of-mean curvature. By analyzing this flow within the framework of degenerate parabolic equations, we establish that the flow remains regular up to its maximal existence time. Additionally, we prove that the flow persists smoothly as $t$ approaches infinity and converges to a round sphere.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image classification, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This paper investigates the frequency domain characteristics of CNNs and their impact on classification outcomes. We introduce a novel framework for training CNNs directly within the frequency domain, where a convolutional layer is defined by its spectrum of Fourier coefficients. Our findings indicate that the frequency-domain representation of CNNs offers significant interpretability, allowing for the identification of the specific frequency features each network prioritizes for classification. Additionally, we demonstrate that frequency-domain training accelerates convergence and reduces training time while maintaining classification accuracy comparable to standard methods.

Unsupervised image clustering is a fundamental task in computer vision that has garnered significant attention from researchers. While deep learning has recently emerged as a leading approach for this domain, it often suffers from overfitting and poor generalization when applied to small datasets. To address these limitations, we introduce a new clustering framework called DeepCluE, which leverages multi-layer ensembles within a deep neural network architecture. This approach utilizes a deep learning model to extract features from input images and employs a multi-layer ensemble strategy to group those images. The DeepCluE system is evaluated on standard benchmark datasets, specifically the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 sets. Experimental findings indicate that DeepCluE outperforms existing state-of-the-art clustering methods.

Identifying risks is essential for institutional decision-making, yet it is frequently hindered by the labor-intensive nature of scanning and analyzing vast quantities of unstructured data. To address this, we introduce a framework that leverages natural language processing and knowledge graphs to automatically detect risk factors and construct risk networks. This system employs a specialized risk dictionary to extract risk factors from news articles, utilizing a knowledge graph to organize these factors and their interrelations. By applying network analysis, the framework identifies the most significant risk factors, which are then integrated into a risk network. This network is subsequently merged with a risk scorecard to generate a comprehensive risk profile. We validated this approach using data from the 2018-2021 period on 1,000 non-financial companies, demonstrating that the method successfully highlights prominent risk factors and produces accurate risk profiles.

Topological Data Analysis (TDA) is a novel methodology designed to extract insights from datasets by capturing their intrinsic topological characteristics. This study introduces a classification framework that leverages TDA to categorize data into distinct groups. The methodology employs a persistent homology matrix to encode the topological features of the data, subsequently utilizing a Random Forest algorithm to derive features for the classification task. The proposed system was evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results indicate that this approach achieves competitive performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

ContraSIMILARITY is defined as an equivalence relation on a finite set that remains invariant under the permutation of two distinct elements, provided they are not adjacent. This work demonstrates that such similiarity partitions correspond exactly to the equilibrium states of certain two-player permutation games characterized by specific properties. Leveraging this game-theoretic interpretation, we offer an intuitive explanation for why the count of contrasimilar classes matches the number of fixed points within the corresponding permutation, and we also provide an accessible proof showing these relations are transitive.

We provide a key representation of the string 2-group established in reference [arXiv:0804.1784], which generalizes the well-known string group's representation as the connected cover of $SO(n)$. This study further examines how the group's 2-representation restricts and relates to ordinary group representations through specific functorial constructions.

The study examines the formation of ion-acoustic mode rogue waves within a double plasma composed of non-ideal electron-positron pairs alongside cold ions. By applying the modified equation of reductive potential, researchers analyzed how rogue wave generation is influenced by the plasma's physical parameters. The analysis reveals that these waves are characterized by an exceptionally high amplitude and a brief duration. Furthermore, it was found that altering the bulk parameters of the plasma can either amplify or diminish the amplitude of the emerging rogue waves.

The parametric decay of Alfvén waves is a primary mechanism for particle heating and acceleration in space plasmas. This study investigates the conditions under which this instability arises within a laboratory plasma, specifically examining how the instability's growth rate and the wavelength of the daughter waves depend on the amplitude of the mother wave, the mother wave's wavelength, and the plasma's Alfvén velocity. To achieve this, we employed a hybrid kinetic-particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation code, which models ion motion kinetically while treating electrons as a fluid. Our results indicate that the instability's growth rate increases with higher mother wave amplitudes and decreases as the mother wave's wavelength expands. Furthermore, daughter wave wavelengths are observed to be approximately twice the length of the mother wave's wavelength.

We investigate the gravitational instability of filamentary molecular clouds by analyzing the dispersion relation of their self-gravitating perturbations. Our analysis reveals that the radial profile of the cloud's density distribution is governed by the wavelength of the most unstable mode, which is notably sensitive to the cloud's magnetic field strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the radial density profile exhibits a double-peaked structure, with the separation between peaks increasing as the strength of the magnetic field grows.

We investigate the quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects within the strong coupling regime, specifically examining a two-level system coupled to a bosonic bath. Our findings indicate that when the system-bath interaction is of the dipolar type, the anti-Zeno effect is impossible. Conversely, under a dipole-square interaction, the effects' dependence on the observation interval is governed by the initial system-bath configuration, and under certain conditions, the anti-Zeno effect is feasible.

This study examines the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model incorporating Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya (DM) interactions and an inhomogeneous external magnetic field. By applying the mean-field approximation, we derive the system's reduced density matrix and calculate the corresponding diagonal and off-diagonal elements of the thermal density matrix. Our results demonstrate that the diagonal terms align with those of the transverse Ising model, whereas the off-diagonal terms are influenced by the DM interaction. Furthermore, we analyze the temperature dependence of the off-diagonal elements, identifying a critical temperature at which they vanish.

This study introduces a distributed trajectory planning framework for quadrotor swarms that ensures collision avoidance. The method employs a linear safe corridor (LSC) to define a bounded region around each agent, where this corridor is constructed based on the current trajectory of the nearest neighbor. By utilizing this constraint, the original non-convex collision avoidance challenge is transformed into a convex Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). The resulting MILP is designed to be solvable in real-time, with its feasibility guaranteed by the proposed construction of the LSC. The approach also offers a formal proof of collision-free operation. Simulation results demonstrate the algorithm's efficacy in generating smooth trajectories for the swarm while strictly adhering to collision avoidance requirements.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has recently gained significant traction in lane detection, offering a viable solution to the challenge of transferring models trained on simulated data to real-world scenarios. This approach is particularly valuable for autonomous driving applications, where training exclusively on real-world data is often impractical due to the high costs associated with data collection and the scarcity of available datasets. In this study, we introduce CARLANE, a comprehensive benchmark for UDA lane detection that includes three distinct real-world datasets: Highway, Urban, and Rural. These datasets are derived from the Cityscapes, BDD100K, and KITTI datasets, respectively, and feature manually annotated lane markings. We further evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art UDA techniques on CARLANE, providing a detailed analysis of their strengths and limitations. The results indicate that these methods can effectively bridge the domain gap between simulation and real-world environments.

The study examines how the spreading and contact line dynamics of water are altered by the presence of suspended particles. Specifically, the receding contact angle (RCA) was measured for water droplets on hydrogels swollen with either pure water or water containing 10% glycerol or 50% glycerol. The RCA values for droplets on pure water were found to be significantly lower than those on glycerol-modified solutions. Furthermore, the RCA behavior varied based on the particle type: while the addition of hydrophobic particles increased the RCA, the inclusion of hydrophilic particles decreased it. These findings are attributed to the distinct wetting characteristics of the particles, which influence the contact line dynamics.

This study examines the link between student connectivity and academic performance using data from a cohort of 1,000 learners at a university during the 2020–2021 pandemic period. The research focuses on the correlation between students' online engagement and their GPA, as well as the identification of distinct student groups characterized by varying levels of both connectivity and academic success. The findings indicate that online presence correlates with grade point average, and the proposed clustering analysis successfully categorizes students into four distinct profiles: disengaged, socially connected but low-achieving, highly engaged with high-achieving, and socially connected but low-achieving. The authors conclude that the observed behavioral patterns and academic outcomes remain consistent with those recorded in the pre-pandemic era.

This study introduces a new approach for deriving vertical wind profiles from L-band Doppler radar data. The method employs an autoregressive model to interpolate the raw radar data, which is then integrated into the Doppler radar equation. This framework allows for the estimation of both wind speed and the correlation time scale. The technique was validated using data from the L-band radar at the Southern Great Plains (SGP) site, which recorded a wind correlation time scale of approximately 10 seconds and a wind speed profile ranging from 10 to 1000 meters. The results demonstrate that this approach yields wind speed estimates with an accuracy of roughly 1 m/s and a correlation time scale within 1 second.

We present a detailed study of UBC 274, a disrupting open cluster located in the Galactic anticenter. Using the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3/UVIS instrument, we obtained a high-resolution image of the cluster's core, which was subsequently analyzed with the DAOPHOT/PHOTOMETER photometric package. This analysis yielded a catalog of 1,000 stars, including 500 identified as cluster members. By examining the color-magnitude diagram (CMD), we determined that UBC 274 is a young, metal-rich cluster with an age of 1.2 ± 0.1 Gyr and a metallicity of [Fe/H] = +0.20 ± 0.05. The cluster's age aligns with the ages of its neighboring clusters, UBC 273 and UBC 275, suggesting a common origin. Kinematical analysis via the Gaia DR2 catalog revealed that UBC 274 exhibits a significant velocity dispersion of 10.5 ± 0.5 km/s, indicating a dynamically hot stellar population. This dispersion is consistent with the high velocity dispersions observed in UBC 273 and UBC 275, further supporting the hypothesis that these three clusters formed together.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved significant success in translation tasks, yet the quality of the resulting text can be suboptimal. Given that NMT models are trained on parallel bitexts, it is logical to hypothesize that enhancing the quality of the input bitexts would consequently improve the output quality. This study investigates whether synthetic translation techniques can refine bitext quality. We evaluate two such methods: back-translation and cross-lingual sentence embedding. Experimental results indicate that while back-translation yields marginal improvements, the sentence embedding approach achieves more substantial gains. Specifically, the embedding-based method elevates BLEU scores by 1.5 and 1.6 points on the WMT14 En-de and En-fr datasets, respectively.

We introduce a dissipative model for interacting spin chains, wherein engineered dissipation drives a transition from a normal state to an entangled steady state. This phenomenon is characterized by a shift in entanglement entropy scaling from logarithmic to a constant (area law) across a finite temperature range. Furthermore, the system's steady-state dynamics are governed by the competition between dissipation and energy-conserving noise.

We examine the spin-orbit coupling within transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayer flat bands, demonstrating that the interlayer hopping between these bands induces an effective spin-orbit interaction. This coupling is characterized by a term that mixes spins parallel and antiparallel to the plane, alongside a perpendicular spin-flipping component. We analyze the impact of this spin-dependent coupling on the magneto-optical properties of the system, specifically focusing on the Zeeman splitting of the exciton spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the interlayer spin-flipping term generates a significant magnetic field-dependent shift in the exciton energy, a phenomenon that can be detected through magneto-optical spectroscopy.

We introduce a quantum reservoir computing framework based on a non-unitary, finite-dimensional quantum map. This approach is realized through a measurement-based implementation of a non-deterministic quantum channel. We demonstrate that the system achieves a universal approximation capability, supported by a rigorous proof of its universality. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the system's stability and its potential for application within a quantum reservoir architecture.

We propose a method for stably trapping neutral atoms using a GaN-on-sapphire chip integrated with a microfabricated electrode array. This approach offers the benefits of high thermal conductivity, robust mechanical strength, and superior optical transparency. We estimate the temperature distribution within the chip and calculate the magnitude of temperature-induced dipole forces acting on the trapped atoms. Furthermore, we analyze the feasibility of integrating optical components directly onto the chip surface and simulating microstructured electrode arrays.

This study evaluates the performance of Lagrange and mixed finite element methods for solving Poisson's equation, employing the open-source library MFEM. The results indicate that both methodological approaches yield comparable efficiency.

This study examines a specific class of sign-changing interactions within dark energy cosmology, where the interaction term is defined as $Q = 3H\beta(H^2-\rho_m)$, with $H$ representing the Hubble parameter, $\rho_m$ representing the matter density, and $\beta$ being a constant. We investigate the model's dynamical evolution and cosmological implications, including the determination of the equation of state for dark energy and dark matter, alongside an analysis of their interdependence. Furthermore, we evaluate the model's viability through stability analysis, phase-space dynamics, and the statefinder diagnostic. Our findings indicate that this sign-changing interaction model is viable and capable of describing the universe's accelerated expansion.

The radio flares observed in tidal disruption events (TDEs) are widely believed to originate from relativistic jets powered by newly formed black holes. While these events are typically viewed as highly relativistic, the radio emission from TDEs can also be explained by a distinct mechanism: particle acceleration within quasi-perpendicular shocks. This process occurs when the jet interacts with the ambient interstellar medium, generating shocks that are effectively perpendicular to the magnetic field lines. We propose that particles gain energy through a hybrid mechanism combining shock acceleration and wave-particle interactions, specifically involving the cyclotron resonance of Alfvén waves. This model successfully reproduces the observed spectral and temporal characteristics of TDE radio flares, including the "hard-to-soft" spectral evolution and the "double-horned" light curve. Furthermore, the model predicts that the radio flares from TDEs should exhibit polarization degrees ranging from 10% to 30%, which can be verified by future observations.

Acoustic cavitation is a phenomenon where the resonant collapse of microbubbles generates extreme local conditions, including high temperatures, pressures, and cavitation nuclei. This process is critical for applications ranging from medical therapies to the generation of chemical products. This study presents a time-domain analysis of cavitation within a microbubbler, revealing that bubble resonance is significantly influenced by the surrounding medium's acoustic properties. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the microbubbler's geometry and material composition substantially affect the system's overall acoustic response.

Detecting stress is crucial for both clinical and human-computer interaction applications. While existing methods typically rely on a single modality, such as audio, facial expressions, or physiological signals, they often fail to achieve high accuracy due to the inherent limitations of relying on a single data source. To address this, we introduce MUSER (Multimodal UNsupervised stress REgulation), a novel framework designed to identify stress in spontaneous human activities by leveraging unlabelled emotion recognition as an auxiliary task. Our approach utilizes a multimodal architecture that simultaneously processes audio, visible, and physiological inputs. To enhance performance, we implement a two-stage training strategy: first, a stress recognition model is trained jointly with an emotion classifier in a multi-task setting; second, the model is fine-tuned exclusively on stress detection labels. Experimental results demonstrate that MUSER surpasses state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a 10.5% increase in F1-score and a 13.4% increase in AUC compared to the leading baseline.

PanGCEA is a versatile toolkit designed for panoramic graph environments, which are increasingly prevalent in applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality. This system offers a comprehensive collection of resources including pre-built panoramic maps, specialized panoramic graph structures, and tailored annotation tools. To support the annotation of panoramic maps, PanGCEA provides a flexible, open-source 3D scene editor capable of handling various panoramic formats. Additionally, the toolkit includes a panoramic graph visualizer designed for the inspection and analysis of panoramic maps.

The "downsizing" phenomenon describes the trend where massive elliptical galaxies (EGGs) cease forming stars earlier than lower-mass galaxies. This study examines the downsizing trend by analyzing the star formation timescales of EGGs using the SDSS-DR7 dataset. We employed a novel approach that accounts for the environment-dependent metallicity of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the frequency of Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) within the galaxies. Our findings indicate that the downsizing effect is more pronounced than previously thought, with the quenching epoch occurring roughly 1.5 billion years earlier than earlier estimates. Additionally, we observed that the star formation timescale of EGGs is significantly influenced by the metallicity of the ISM and the number of SNIa events.

This study introduces a new approach to image compressive sensing reconstruction utilizing non-convex regularization. The proposed method leverages the sparse representation of images within overcomplete dictionaries, specifically those exhibiting group sparsity characteristics. To achieve this, we integrate a novel non-convex model with a group sparsity prior, which is then solved using an efficient algorithm. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence of this algorithm, and numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both image quality and reconstruction fidelity.

The widespread adoption of smartphones has driven the surge in popularity of skin analysis applications, which typically rely on deep learning to detect skin issues within images. However, these existing methods often struggle with the inherent diversity of skin conditions, resulting in subpar performance. To address this, we introduce RethNet, a new deep learning architecture designed to identify specific lesions within facial images. RethNet operates by first segmenting the image into individual objects and subsequently classifying each object to determine the presence of a skin problem. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art models, achieving a 10% increase in mAP and a 5% increase in accuracy on the FaceSkin dataset.

PAC codes are a class of quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check codes that are currently being evaluated for integration into the fifth-generation (5G) standard. This research examines the performance and computational complexity of sequential decoding for these codes. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a specific representation of the parity check matrix that enables the tracing of variable node paths within the corresponding Tanner graph. Leveraging this representation, we derive a closed-form expression for the average computational load of the bit-flipping algorithm. Additionally, we establish a closed-form expression for the mutual information between transmitted and received sequences under a binary erasure channel. Finally, we evaluate the decoding performance of PAC codes using a simulated bit-flipping approach.

Sequential recommendation systems are designed to forecast a user's next item preference based on their historical interactions. However, their performance often degrades for cold-start users possessing minimal interaction history. While existing methods attempt to address this by transferring knowledge from similar users, they fail to account for the inherent sequential nature of user behavior. To overcome this limitation, we introduce STLM, a novel sequential cold-start recommendation framework. STLM leverages meta-learning to establish a robust base representation for users with scarce data by utilizing a meta-learner trained on diverse users with varying interaction counts. This approach effectively transfers knowledge from both highly active and moderately active users to benefit cold-start individuals. Furthermore, we incorporate a meta-structural transition module that captures the underlying structure of user behavior sequences, thereby enhancing the model's ability to predict recommendations. Empirical evaluations across three standard benchmarks confirm that STLM significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 10.1% improvement in Hit Rate and 13.8% improvement in MRR for cold-start scenarios.

This paper examines the current state of research in ultra-high energy cosmic ray (UHECR) physics. It briefly outlines the origins of UHECRs, their acceleration mechanisms, and the phenomena related to their propagation and detection. The work also addresses the ultra-high energy neutrino flux and the significance of their detection.

The DART mission represents the inaugural active planetary defense test, aiming to alter the orbit of the Didymos moonlet by impacting it with the kinetic DART spacecraft. This study examines how the projectile's shape influences momentum transfer, specifically analyzing the crater size and morphology resulting from impacts on the moonlet. We conducted experiments using 10 mm and 20 mm aluminum spheres and cylinders dropped onto a 1 mm aluminum sheet at velocities between 1.5 and 3.0 m/s. These experimental results were compared with numerical simulations performed using the SPH code, which modeled the impact of 10 mm and 20 mm aluminum spheres and cylinders at 5.0 km/s onto a 10 cm copper target. The study found that, for a given mass, spherical projectiles yield the highest crater dimensions, while cylindrical shapes produce the lowest. This finding aligns with the observed differences in the dimensionless crater diameter ($\Delta$) between the two geometries. Additionally, the research indicates that the momentum transfer coefficient ($\mu$) is independent of both impact velocity and the target's material strength. These insights offer valuable context for interpreting the DART mission's impact results and calculating the momentum transfer coefficient.

Driver recognition is a critical component of driver monitoring systems, serving as a key safety feature for vehicles. However, achieving this indoors is often difficult due to the lack of sufficient lighting, and the challenge is even greater in outdoor settings where visibility is severely compromised by strong sunlight. To address these issues, this study introduces a driver recognition framework that integrates two distinct deep neural networks: one optimized for low-light conditions and the other for high-light conditions. The approach employs a new method called the Mertens Unrolled Network (MU-Net) to fuse the outputs of these networks. This fusion process utilizes the rapid convergence of the RRM algorithm, which is a computationally efficient technique for calculating high dynamic range (HDR) images. The proposed MU-Network is a computationally efficient, unrolled network designed to achieve high performance. Extensive experiments conducted on the Driver Recognition in Safety Systems (DRIVE) dataset demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

The Comprehensive Blub Archive Network (CBA-N) is introduced as a new framework for constructing open-source programming language repositories, developed through qualitative interviews with repository maintainers and repository engineers. This approach synthesizes the insights gained from these participants into twelve distinct design principles. The CBA Network is structured around three core components: the Blub Archive, which serves as the primary repository for source code; the Developer Forum, which facilitates communication and collaboration; and the Code Review Team, which ensures quality assurance. The paper outlines the specific design principles and illustrates how the CBA Network can be implemented to effectively build open-source language repositories.

This study addresses the problem of estimating average treatment effects in scenarios involving incomplete data for covariates and outcomes, utilizing inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) combined with propensity score models. We introduce a novel estimator designed to enhance robustness and efficiency by integrating multiple propensity score estimators. This approach is demonstrated to be equivalent to optimal linear combinations of the individual propensity score models. Furthermore, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed method, providing guidance for constructing confidence intervals. The study also includes a simulation analysis to compare the performance of our estimator against existing methods.

This paper examines the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, denoted as $K(k)$. We establish two inequalities involving $K(k)$ and $\text{arccosh}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-k^2}-1}\right)$, valid for the range $0 < k < 1$. Additionally, for the same domain, we derive a sharp double inequality bounding these integral and term with a parameterized factor $(1+r_k)$.

This paper addresses the challenge of deriving inductive procedures from input-output examples. We introduce a novel framework that breaks down this complex task into simpler subproblems, each solvable using established learning methods. Our framework is designed to be flexible, allowing the integration of diverse existing techniques. We validate our approach on a comprehensive set of problems from the Synthesis and Automated Theorem- Proving (SYNTH) competition. Our experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 100-fold improvement in performance.

The rise of social media has created a fertile environment for the spread of fake news, which can be manipulated or generated by automated systems. This study introduces an innovative approach to automatically produce fake news in Arabic, utilizing a unique dataset created through a hybrid method that combines paraphrasing with a language model. The research evaluates the effectiveness of this hybrid-generated dataset against one created exclusively via a language model. The findings indicate that content paraphrasing significantly enhances the quality of the generated fake news. Additionally, the study assesses the performance of various machine learning classifiers in distinguishing between genuine and fabricated news. The research concludes by discussing the implications of these results for countering fake news dissemination.

In this paper, we determine the possible torsion subgroups for elliptic curves defined over the compositum of all $D_4$ extensions of the rational numbers. Building on an assumption made by some of the coauthors in a prior publication, we provide evidence supporting its validity. Additionally, we offer descriptions of further results that could be achieved if the time permits.

This study investigates the nonlocal correlations within an open system comprising $N$ qubits, where each qubit interacts with its own independent environment. We analyze how these correlations evolve over time, considering scenarios in which the initial density matrix of the $N$-qubit system is either separable or entangled. Our findings indicate that regardless of whether the initial state is separable or entailed, the nonlocal correlations decay over time and eventually vanish in the long run. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these correlations can be modeled using a matrix product operator (MPO) representation.

Focused crawling involves navigating the web to identify specific content, such as articles discussing a particular subject or websites offering specific services. This paper introduces a new focused crawler that employs a tree-based strategy and Q-learning to locate target pages. The approach begins by selecting a set of seed pages that serve as the starting point. Next, it applies a method called the "crawling tree" to prioritize pages for indexing. This technique ranks pages by assigning higher scores to those that are either direct neighbors of seed pages or have already been visited. Additionally, it assigns a score reflecting how closely each unvisited page aligns with the crawling objective. To optimize this process, the paper utilizes a Q-learning algorithm to train the scoring functions. This algorithm enables the system to learn the most effective way to score unvisited pages and aligns the visited-node score function with the alignment metric for unvisited nodes. The proposed method was evaluated against several existing focused crawling algorithms using a dataset of news websites. The experimental results demonstrate that the new approach outperforms the competing methods.

Event data has become ubiquitous across numerous domains, including healthcare, manufacturing, and finance. However, event-oriented systems face significant challenges due to data heterogeneity, which arises from diverse entities generating events with varying attributes and even different types. While existing literature has extensively examined handling heterogeneity at the individual event level, it has largely overlooked the necessity of grouping events into cases and variants. This paper addresses that gap by introducing a formal framework for cases and variants within event-driven systems. We define a case as a specific instance of a process modeled by a process model, while a variant represents a recurring pattern of events that occurs repeatedly throughout a case. The paper also explores the challenges associated with discovering these structures in event data and presents a formal method for automatically identifying them.

This study introduces a novel matrix decomposition technique for recovering missing seismic data, specifically targeting the challenging scenarios of dense sampling gaps. The proposed approach, termed "subspace-constrained weighted matrix completion," is built upon the established weighted matrix completion framework. It integrates a subspace constraint into the weighted matrix factorization process, thereby enforcing a specific subspace structure on the recovered wavefield. This method is particularly effective for dense grids where traditional interpolation techniques struggle due to the high number of missing entries. We demonstrate that the proposed formulation maintains the core advantages of matrix completion while ensuring the solution resides within a constrained, physically plausible subspace. Numerical experiments confirm that the method achieves high accuracy in reconstructing wavefields and exhibits robustness against noise.

Metalenses are promising for enabling compact, high-performance optical systems, yet their performance is often constrained by narrow bandwidths and limited fields of view. This study introduces a broadband metalens capable of operating over an octave frequency range from 400 to 800 THz and supporting a wide 80° field of view. The lens utilizes a quadratic phase profile to achieve this performance. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that quadratic phase metasurfaces can maintain a narrow beam waist and a low wavefront curvature factor across both high and low frequencies, even with large fields of view. Theoretical results are validated through rigorous coupled-wave analysis and finite-difference time-domain simulations. The resulting broad spectral response is attributed to the quadratic phase's inherent ability to accommodate frequency scaling, which effectively mitigates the impacts of diffraction and wavefront curvature variations.

This study introduces a two-dimensional, non-neutral, fluid model designed to simulate radio frequency (RF) atmospheric-pressure helium plasma jets. The model accounts for the spatial and temporal variations of electric fields, electron density, and neutral gas temperature, while incorporating a newly developed analytical framework for electron transport coefficients. By applying this model to a 13.56 MHz RF system, we demonstrate that electron density fluctuations occur at the RF frequency, while the electron gas temperature remains quasi-steady. Furthermore, we show that including the temperature dependence of electron mobility and thermal conductivity is essential for accurately predicting the spatial distribution of electron density. Finally, our simulation results align well with experimental data, validating the model's predictive capabilities.

This study investigates the quasinormal modes (QNM) of scalar perturbations within the shadow of $d$-dimensional black holes incorporating string theory corrections, utilizing a TeVeS-inspired scalar-tensor framework. By applying the WKB approximation to the effective potential, we determine the QNM frequencies for scalar fields. Furthermore, we examine the influence of the tensor mode coupling parameter $\beta$ on these frequencies. Our results indicate that the QNM frequencies are directly proportional to the scalar field mass.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are currently the premier method for detecting nanohertz-frequency gravitational waves (GWs). These signals are characterized by a distinctive sky- and time-dependent cross-correlation pattern between pairs of pulsars, a feature that arises from the specific propagation of GWs through the Milky Way and the Earth's motion. This paper demonstrates that such correlations can be extracted from data even when the underlying GWs are not common across the entire array. We achieve this by modeling the GWs as a common-spectrum stochastic process composed of multiple, uncorrelated Gaussian processes, each with its own amplitude and frequency. This framework is then extended to scenarios where the GWs are not isotropic. Our approach is validated using simulated data from the NANOGrav 9-pulsar set, successfully recovering the correct GW amplitudes and frequencies. Furthermore, we confirm that the recovered spatial correlations align with theoretical expectations. These findings indicate that our method is applicable to both current and future PTA collaborations.

This paper establishes novel necessary and sufficient conditions for support constraints in generators of linear codes, utilizing the concept of a Hamming weight matrix. Specifically, if $A$ denotes a support matrix for an $A$-free space $V$, and $B$ represents a support matrix for a subspace $U \subseteq V$, then $A$ is contained in $B$ if and only if $A$ is a submatrix of $B$. This result is applied to construct optimal linear codes under specific support constraints.

This study examines a sender's optimal strategy for persuading a Bayesian receiver regarding the validity of a new drug, where the sender possesses superior information. The receiver must decide whether to approve the drug based on a sequential series of clinical trials, with each test outcome informing the subsequent phase. We employ Bayesian persuasion to determine the sender's optimal testing strategy and the corresponding value of this persuasion power. Our findings reveal that the strategic value of conducting tests diminishes as the receiver's initial prior belief in the drug's efficacy approaches either extreme (high approval or high rejection).

Unsupervised audio anomaly detection is a critical task with broad applications, such as identifying gunshots or glass breakages. While recent advances in deep learning have significantly enhanced performance in this area, supervised methods remain the standard due to their superior results. However, the scarcity of labeled audio data often restricts the practicality of supervised approaches. This study investigates the efficacy of unsupervised detection by analyzing various deep learning architectures, specifically examining how their performance degrades when trained on audio from one domain and tested on audio from a different domain. Our findings indicate that unsupervised methods can achieve comparable results to supervised ones, provided the training and testing audio domains are sufficiently similar.

This work investigates itinerant ferromagnetism within dilute three-dimensional SU(N) Fermi gases. We demonstrate that when a repulsive Fermi gas is tuned from strong to weak interactions, ferromagnetism vanishes and transitions into a paramagnetic state. Utilizing the Hubbard-Slater exchange field theory, we calculate the critical impurity concentration ($x_c$) for the onset of this transition. Our findings indicate that $x_c$ decreases as interaction strength weakens, becoming vanishingly small in the thermal regime. Furthermore, we find that $x_c$ diminishes as either the scattering length or the number of internal spin components (N) increases.

We examined the pulsars' emission characteristics across various energies, including their pulse profiles, and investigated potential correlations with their spin-down rates. We also explored the possibility of a link between the pulsars' spin-down rates and their dispersion measures.
